rounds.proof_sketch: The mutation changes shared memory allocation from 256 to 257 elements. With block_size=256 and tid ∈ [0,255], all accesses are: (1) shared_sums[tid] for writes (indices 0-255), (2) shared_sums[tid+stride] for reads where max index is 127+128=255 in the first reduction step. Both original (256 elements) and mutated (257 elements) arrays are sufficient for indices 0-255. The extra element at index 256 is never accessed.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation only increases the shared memory array size from 256 to 257 elements without changing any index calculations, loop bounds, or arithmetic operations. Since blockDim.x=256, thread IDs range from 0 to 255, and all shared memory accesses use indices within [0,255]. The parallel reduction's maximum access pattern is tid+stride where the highest value is 127+128=255 during the first iteration. The 257th element (index 256) is never read or written, making the mutation semantically equivalent to the original. No input values can trigger different behavior because the computational logic is unchanged.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable. The mutation adds unused memory space without affecting any computation. Both kernels produce identical results for all possible inputs because the extra array element is never accessed.
rounds.recommendations: For mutation testing of shared memory array sizes, focus on mutations that either: (1) reduce array size below required capacity causing out-of-bounds access, (2) change indexing logic, or (3) affect synchronization barriers. Mutations that only increase unused capacity are semantically equivalent and should be filtered by static equivalence detection rules.
